items.summary: GPT-6.2 Astra takes the crown but bad at software engineering, Gemini 4 Neon is an impressive improvement from Google but still overrated, Fable 5.2 is smart but expensive, and new Chinese models as well
items.story_key: story|title:evaluating recent model releases on gdpx
items.content_excerpt: Earlier this month we released GDPx , a benchmark designed to measure the domains most valuable for frontier intelligence. Most agentic benchmarks only measure a single domain like coding or legal. The few that try to be comprehensive, like GDPVal or Agent’s Last Exam , make the mistake of selecting domains based on percentage of GDP or the O*NET taxonomy. AI’s impact is nowhere near evenly distributed across the economy today, and we expect this trend to intensify in the future. Many tasks already can’t justify paying for Fable 5.2, much less Fable 7. Thus, if your goal is to track the progress of frontier models, you should focus on the domains where they will be most impactful. It’s for this reason that GDPx intentionally forgoes industries like government and real estate, and instead covers the following domains: Our methodology is also unique. To ensure all our tasks are truly representative of their respective domains, we partnered with 14 specialized data partners to make 206 tasks. The single most notable thing about GDPx, however, is its difficulty. Whereas other benchmarks will often debut with the top model scoring over 50%, Opus 5.5—the highest-scoring model on release day—scored just 12% on GDPx. This massive headroom is what allows GDPx to discriminate between future model releases, unlike saturated benchmarks such as Terminal Bench 4.0 . SemiAnalysis is hiring for GDPx! If you’re interested in helping cement GDPx v2 as the world’s best benchmark, reach out to gdpx@semianalysis.com. Since launching GDPx on November 1st, both Anthropic and OpenAI have released new frontier models. Google made a dramatic resurgence with the Gemini 4 series, and we’ve seen notable releases from Alibaba and Moonshot as well. The GDPx leaderboard now looks like this: It’s worth emphasizing that certain models like Fable 5.2 and GPT-6.2 Astra have sandbagged overall scores due to their safety classifiers. If we exclude cyber, biology, and alignment, the three domains where safety classifiers sometimes kick in, and switch to partial grading to get more signal from the extremely difficult legal and finance domains (which default to binary grading), we get the following leaderboard instead. We think you can argue either of these is the “correct” GDPx leaderboard. On one hand, safety classifiers truly limit the usefulness of models in domains like cyber and bio. items.title: Agent-as-a-Verifier: From Scores to Evidence for General Verification
items.summary: Verification is increasingly critical across various inference and learning paradigms, such as test-time scaling, recursive intelligence and automated research, where feedback can improve efficiency and optimization. Common score-based verifiers, or discriminative reward models, predict a scalar reward for an output. While useful for filtering, rewarding, and ranking, such scores provide no explicit, auditable evidentiary basis for the judgment. In parallel, although existing generative process reward models offer text feedback, most designs do not fully exploit agentic capabilities, such as tool use and iterative reasoning, which are essential for fact-checking and fine-grained claim verification. In this paper, we address these limitations by introducing Agent-as-a-Verifier, an agentic, certificate-producing verification system that places role-separated LLM agents inside a formal-methods-inspired claim-obligation-certificate protocol. Given a generation candidate, Agent-as-a-Verifier produces a certificate by extracting a verdict-blind dependency graph of claims, independently compiling the task's acceptance contract, and deriving checkable obligations. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, Agent-as-a-Verifier achieves higher accuracy than the state-of-the-art approach. Across different downstream applications, the augmented agent also outperforms the plain agent on FrontierMath and CyberGym. More importantly, Agent-as-a-Verifier is able to identify reward-hacking solutions that deceive the benchmark evaluator, highlighting its broader potential for iterative and recursive agent optimization. Code is available at https://github.com/sunyxedu/General-Verifier

items.title: DRBench Pro: A Knowledge-Centric Benchmark for Professional Deep Research Agents
items.summary: Deep research agents gather information from multiple sources and synthesize it into reports on complex, open-ended questions. Existing benchmarks assess report quality along several dimensions, but lack a dedicated knowledge-centric evaluation of which research directions a report covers and how deeply it explores them. We introduce DRBench Pro, a benchmark that makes structured knowledge coverage the primary evaluation target. Our automated pipeline builds local knowledge trees from Wikipedia and uses sampled subgraphs to generate research queries and evidence-grounded rubrics. Each rubric corresponds to a relation in the tree, preserving the structure of the knowledge being evaluated. Agents receive only the research query. This structure allows us to measure breadth across major research directions and depth along related knowledge chains, with their geometric mean giving overall coverage. The benchmark includes 144 cases across 24 domains and 44,102 rubrics. Evaluating 16 deep research agents reveals different strengths in breadth and depth, with the best-performing agent reaching 57.04% overall coverage. Rubric judgments agree closely with human annotations, and agent rankings remain stable across the tested metric configurations.

items.title: Latent-in-the-Middle: On the Security of Cross-Model Latent Communication in Multi-Agent Systems
items.summary:
As large language models increasingly collaborate in heterogeneous multi-agent systems, latent communication has emerged as an efficient alternative to exchanging natural-language messages. By sharing internal representations, agents can avoid repeatedly processing the same context, reducing communication overhead and prefill computation. One such mechanism is cross-model Key-Value (KV) cache transfer, which uses a learned mapper to translate a source model's KV cache into one a target model can use. However, this handoff means the target model consumes context it did not encode itself, thus calling into question whether its safety alignment still holds.
  In this work, we investigate the security implications of latent handoffs by introducing Chasm, a framework characterizing cross-model handoff attacks across three new attack surfaces: the source model, mapper, and handoff mechanism itself. Our experiments reveal that latent handoffs substantially undermine safety alignment and prompt-injection defenses. Notably, a target model that follows only 0.4% of benchmark prompt injections natively, follows up to 44.2% when transferred through a mapper from a source model. On the other hand, for jailbreak attacks, transfer alone raises attack success by up to 24.6 pp within a model family and zero-shot attacks by up to 69.2 pp, whereas white-box optimization through the mapper boosts the attack success rate to 92.5%, against 37.5% for ordinary GCG on the same target. To address these vulnerabilities, we propose a lightweight target-side cache guard that corrects transferred caches to restore the target model's refusal, considerably mitigating these attacks.

items.title: Models Alone Aren't Enough: Connected Context for Agents | Alan Braun, Atlassian
items.summary:
AI is making individuals faster, but few companies can point to org-wide returns. Alan Braun, VP of Product for Ecosystem, AI & Developer Platforms at Atlassian, argues that AI outcomes equal context times intelligence, and that the missing piece is connected context across teams, tools and agents. He shows how Atlassian's Teamwork Graph links knowledge, work, code, people and data, shares lessons from building MCP tools, and demos a coding agent planning with and without connected context. Recorded at AI DevCon New York 2026.

What we cover:
– Why individual AI gains aren't adding up to org-wide returns
– AI outcomes = context × intelligence
– Work spans teams, tools and agents, and the bottleneck has moved
– Context as a graph: seven layers of connected context
– Lessons from building MCP tools around jobs to be done
– Demo: Claude Code with and without connected context

items.title: Announcing vLLM-GR: Efficient Inference for Generative Recommendation
items.summary: vLLM-GR extends vLLM to serve generative recommendation models with accelerator-side beam search, catalog constraints, and shared KV caching across candidate paths.
items.story_key: model:vllm|title:announcing vllm gr efficient inference for generative recommendation
items.content_excerpt: Today we’re introducing vLLM-GR , an open-source inference and serving framework built on vLLM for generative recommendation models. Consider a video feed. Given a viewer’s history, a model such as OneRec can generate a semantic ID (SID) for a video the viewer might watch next. To assemble a feed, the application needs a set of candidates. vLLM-GR extends vLLM’s model execution and paged key-value (KV) cache with beam search that explores multiple candidate IDs in one request. The overview shows how recommendation models generate item IDs or score supplied candidates. The OneRec-1.7B example below follows the generation path, from a viewer’s history to 128 candidate SIDs. A recommendation service has to turn a long interaction history into a set of candidates within a single request’s latency budget. Generating each item ID may take only a few tokens, yet the engine must explore many paths and return items the application can serve. vLLM-GR builds its recommendation search into the vLLM engine. vLLM supplies the scheduler, model execution, and paged KV cache. vLLM-GR adds a beam session that spans the whole search and keeps track of how candidate paths branch. EngineCore owns each beam session from admission to completion. The scheduler dispatches prefill and decode stages to a worker. At each stage, the model runner scores the next token and beam selection records the score and parent of each surviving path. The next decode uses those parent indices to read the right KV state. One request returns two candidates with beam widths of 2 → 3 → 2. The catalog filters out A1 · B1 because no item starts with that prefix. A full-vocabulary search skips this filter. The SIDs and scores are illustrative. In the prefill–decode–decode (PDD) pipeline, the scheduler admits a BeamSearch() request and dispatches its prefill stage to the worker. Prefill scores the first SID component while the host prepares decode 1. During decode 1, the host prepares decode 2. The second decode inherits the selected parents’ suffix KV and completes two SIDs. Green marks the component selected at each stage. The benchmarks measure P99 latency to show how beam width and batch size affect tail latency for generative recommendation. The two overview charts hold the input length at 1,024 tokens and compare beam widths of 256 and 128 at batch sizes 1, 4, and 8 across four NVIDIA GPUs and two Ascend NPUs. items.title: How the Claude Code team thinks about verification
items.summary: How end-to-end, property and differential tests let coding agents verify their work with evidence, and what the Claude Code team does to keep its verifiers honest.
items.story_key: model:claude|title:how the claude code team thinks about verification
items.content_excerpt: How end-to-end, property and differential tests let coding agents verify their work with evidence, and what the Claude Code team does to keep its verifiers honest. On the Claude Code team, the vast majority of our code (~90%) is written and reviewed by Claude . At this scale, how we equip our agents to verify their work with evidence becomes extremely important. Verification loops are the building block that lets you delegate more work to Claude. Without them, you can really only run one or two Claudes at a time, because you have to check everything yourself. With them, you can run dozens or hundreds in parallel. That’s because giving agents a way to verify their output is an effective way to improve quality. In internal testing around structured file generation, having a separate grader check Claude’s work against a rubric improved task success by up to 10 points over a standard prompting loop, with the largest gains on the hardest problems. What was once expensive to verify (tests, benchmarks, specs, real end-to-end runs) is now cheap to request from an agent. Like code, agents can quickly generate tests, benchmarks, and specs. And once generated, these tests and benchmarks run as software so they can be run frequently without using many additional tokens. You can also close the verification loop by using the results to improve the agent’s performance on that task. For example, if an agent repeatedly fails a test that checks logs for user data, you can create a hook or a more explicit rule in your CLAUDE.md to avoid future issues. This (mostly) stops issues from happening again. So if verification is critical to producing quality code at a high velocity, what types of tests should you use and how should you apply them across your pipeline? This article answers those questions and also shares the process used by the Claude Code team. If your tests are flaky you’ll train the agent to run them again rather than fixing the failing code. If your tests are slow, the agent will do fewer tests across batches which can make pinpointing issues difficult. Heavier tests are best deployed before you’ve committed the changes. If you have to focus on one test type, pick end-to-end. These tests describe real user flows like adding an item to a cart, checking out, and moving to a confirmation page. The reason E2E tests are so effective is that they are difficult to fool–either the whole feature works or it doesn't. They also have definitive done criteria and can concrete

items.title: How Much Do Coding Agents Over-Edit, and Why? An Empirical Study of Unneeded Edits in Repository-Level Agent Patches
items.summary: Agent patches are larger than developers', which is widely read as over-editing. But patch size does not say whether the extra edits are needed, what they are, or where they come from. We introduce Delta Residue Attribution (DRA), which replays agent trajectories, traces every block (unit) of the final patch to the step that wrote it, reverts each unit, and reruns the task tests to decide whether the unit is needed. We apply DRA to 7,660 resolved GitHub Copilot CLI trajectories from 18 frontier models on SWE-bench Verified (6,728) and DeepSWE (932), and grade developer patches using the same method. Agent patches do change more lines than developers'; on SWE-bench Verified the majority of extra edits add tests (61%) and documentation (13%) while on DeepSWE, most extra edits are code (58%). On both benchmarks, agents' code is on average at least as necessary as developers' (mean $NP_{code}$ 0.887 vs. 0.864 on SWE-bench Verified, where 11 of 18 models leave less unneeded code than developers, and 0.797 vs. 0.785 on DeepSWE). On average, 11% of an agent patch's code units on SWE-bench Verified are still unneeded, and 89% of those change behavior. Debug steps write almost none of the unneeded code. Code necessity differs substantially by model; it is unrelated to resolve rate on SWE-bench Verified and negatively correlated with it on DeepSWE (Spearman -0.59, p = 0.01). On SWE-bench Verified, pruning with DRA using only the tests the agent can see (its own tests and the repository's) removes the majority of unneeded code but also some needed code (67% recall, 46% precision), and 89% of pruned patches still resolve the task; asking the agent to audit its own diff is more precise but less effective (36% recall, 66% precision). We recommend that benchmarks report code necessity next to resolve rate and that over-editing be addressed through model training and harness-level pruning.

items.title: ConTra: A Training Framework for Effective Contextual Retrieval via Prefix Generation
items.summary: Data management systems organize large text collections for tasks such as finding relevant studies and extracting contract clauses. Systems make long documents searchable by splitting them into independently indexed chunks. Chunking can separate text from its identifying details. The indexing challenge is to keep each chunk independently searchable while preserving the context needed to find and rank it. Existing methods either encode that context in chunk vectors or attach it as a text prefix. Context encoded only in vectors is unavailable to text rerankers. Prompted prefixes serve both vector search and reranking, but are costly to generate at indexing time and can underperform contextual encoders. We propose ConTra (Context That Travels), a reinforcement learning framework for training lightweight prefix generators. Its reward combines feedback from frozen embedding and reranking models with factual verification and length control. ConTra generates one prefix per chunk during index construction and stores the augmented text and its embedding for reuse across queries. To evaluate contextual retrieval across workloads and under interference, we introduce RealContextBench, a benchmark with five application collections and three controlled conditions that isolate the effect of distracting text. On ConTEB and RealContextBench, ConTra-2B outperforms the prompted 9B baseline using Anthropic's method and the PPLX-4B contextual encoder, with a margin of up to 3.15 points over their best overall scores, while indexing short documents 7.74 times and 2.15 times as fast as those baselines, respectively. Post-trained only on ConTEB, it leads the standalone methods on RealContextBench after reranking and is less sensitive than the prompted 2B baseline to random and topically similar distractors. Code, datasets, and trained models are available at https://github.com/SStan1/ConTra.

items.title: Introducing Search for Agents
items.summary: Flip one toggle to make your site searchable by AI agents — complete with automatic content indexing, a discoverable search API, and native HTTP QUERY support.
items.story_key: story|title:introducing search for agents
items.content_excerpt: AI Search , our service that indexes your content and lets you add search to any application or agent without having to build an entire retrieval infrastructure, has supported adding your website as a data source for a while now, automatically crawling, converting and indexing its pages. Still, setting up an AI Search instance for your website requires manually creating and configuring it initially, and then doing all the integration work to get the search endpoints available from your domain and to make sure that agents know where to find the index and know how to use it. Today we're introducing Search for Agents , which puts that setup behind a toggle in your Cloudflare dashboard. Turn it on for your zone, and our service will create your AI Search instance, start indexing your content, and make search discoverable and available from your own domain. The idea follows naturally from Markdown for Agents , where Cloudflare's network converts any HTML page to Markdown in real time for enabled zones using content negotiation headers. Similarly, Search for Agents leverages the power of AI Search by automatically creating an index for your zone and exposing APIs that any AI agent can discover and use to search your website, under your domain, all done at the network level. You can enable Search for Agents using the API, or by going to the dashboard in your zone page, under Quick Actions : Search for Agents is available to all customers, including Free (with limits ). Once it’s enabled, Cloudflare will automatically create an AI Search instance, start crawling and indexing the content in your zone. Refer to our developer documentation to understand how the crawling process works. You can access your instance directly from this page, or by going to directly to your account’s AI > AI Search instances view: The AI Search instance for your zone is created with default settings, but you can enable reranking or change configuration options like cache settings at any time. Refer to our documentation for the full list of options. Once AI Search indexes your content, you or any agent on the Internet can start using Search for Agents, subject to your domain settings (e.g. your bot management settings, AI Crawl Control and web application firewall ( WAF ) configurations). Search isn't much use if the agents don’t know it's there. To facilitate discoverability, Search for Agents automatically advertises the search endpoint on every page of your site. If you also have Markdo

items.title: claude-code v2.1.332
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added skills from MCP servers (beta). They show as server:skill in the / menu; other skills keep their names
  • Added a PreSkillShellCommand hook event that can refuse a skill or command's inline shell commands as it loads; on 2.1.331 and older, a settings file naming it opens a dialog at start
  • Added "Always deliver" to the prompt for held messages from other sessions
  • Added a footer line that stays while a flagged message has your session on a different model, until you pick one with /model
  • Added an OpenTelemetry assistant_response event for text Claude sends through SendUserMessage or Cowork's message tool, when response logging is on
  • Added a warning in VS Code and Desktop's Code tab when part of a session couldn't be saved, saying how to save it with /compact
  • Added a notice in VS Code and Desktop's Code tab when a resumed session's earlier messages weren't loaded, as the terminal already shows
  • Added your Cyber Verification Program access tier to the startup header, beside the model name when your tier applies to that model and you're signed in with a claude.ai account
  • Fixed claude auth login reporting Login successful. when a claude.ai login could not be saved: it now exits 1 and says what to check, such as a leftover lock file or a full disk
  • Fixed Read, @-mentions and compaction hanging on a named pipe that nothing writes to, such as a .env mounted by a locked secrets manager; the read now fails after 20 seconds
  • Fixed turns ending in "Prompt is too long" after repeated auto-compaction failures when one more compaction at the context limit could have kept them going
  • Fixed compaction failing when a summary kept running past the output limit: after three cut-off replies, the last try now asks for a shorter summary
  • Fixed a freeze when a permission rule or hook condition with several wildcards was checked against a long command
  • Fixed freezes and runaway memory use in most cases while a hook prints output without end
  • Fixed a freeze and context overflow when a hook blocks or fails during a turn, or after /compact, with a very large log; text over about 50,000 characters is now shortened
  • Fixed the terminal freezing, and ignoring Ctrl+C, while a local MCP server floods its standard output
  • Fixed a freeze when a prompt or piped input holds an @ followed by a very long unbroken string, such as minified CSS with an embedded font
  • Fixed a long freeze when opening a rewind point after a large tracked file was rewritten
  • Fixed SSE MCP servers hanging or refusing every tool call after their event stream was cut and came back on a new endpoint or not at all, until reconnected by hand
  • Fixed Remote Control showing a session in the desktop app, VS Code or the Agent SDK as running while it waited there on a dialog or an MCP server's question
  • Fixed a usage limit being reported as reached to Remote Control, IDE and SDK clients after it had already reset
  • Fixed CLAUDE.md and rules files being sent to the model a second time, in most cases, after a session moves into a worktree under .claude/worktrees with EnterWorktree or is resumed there
  • Fixed tool calls that never ran being counted as done in a claude.ai chat's summary line after you declined a permission prompt in a session that had restarted
  • Linux: Fixed the Bash edit diff showing an unchanged symlink as edited after Claude had read the file through it
  • Fixed resuming a session and /stats freezing for seconds when a transcript holds many damaged lines
  • Fixed a family name such as sonnet in --fallback-model being dropped when availableModels allows only an older version of it
  • Fixed keys lagging for seconds while /stats reads large session transcripts, also after the dialog is closed, and with debug logging on while a language server floods its stderr
  • Fixed a session failing when the cloud refused its default model and an availableModels list that isn't enforced named neither it nor an older model of that family
  • Fixed an enforced list of older models failing on Google Cloud's Agent Platform and Foundry when the first is refused: it now steps down to the next in that family, if listed newest first
  • Fixed opus failing on Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform and Foundry behind a gateway that refuses a model in its own words: it now steps down to an older model that answers
  • Fixed the start-up model upgrade offer on Bedrock and Google Cloud's Agent Platform naming a model that your availableModels list leaves out
  • Fixed Bedrock sub-agents failing when your account lists no profile for their model in the parent's region: they now use the model's own profile, which can be outside that region
  • Fixed Foundry sessions leaving a model family when an admin's list blocks the version sonnet, opus or haiku points to: they now use its newest allowed version under a built-in or mapped name
  • Fixed the sonnet alias on Bedrock Mantle resolving to Haiku 4.5: it now means Sonnet 5, not Sonnet 5.5, and an account without Sonnet 5 gets an error, so enable it first
  • Fixed Ctrl+C at the prompt starting a new turn, and a double Ctrl+C not exiting, when a background agent it stopped had an unread subagent report
  • Fixed /install-github-app ticking a workflow again after going back with Esc
  • Fixed dictated text past 10,000 characters being lost
  • Fixed raw "JSON Parse error" and "The operation was aborted." API errors when the non-streaming retry got a broken response or was interrupted
  • Fixed Esc not stopping computer use between actions on macOS when Claude Code's window or an app you allowed is in front; an Esc meant for that app's popup now stops computer use instead
  • Fixed a rare hang when a helper command, such as an API key helper, ran past its time limit
  • Fixed selecting text in fullscreen pushing the footer's right-hand label onto a second row, which moved the text under the mouse and could copy the wrong line
  • Fixed a PreToolUse hook's reason for asking not showing on terminal Read, Grep, Glob, Edit and Write prompts (#102892, #105343)
  • Fixed temp_* folders piling up in ~/.claude/plugins/cache when a downloaded plugin couldn't be copied into place
  • Fixed --effort being ignored when starting an interactive session with --environment while CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL is set to the same level
  • Fixed headless and cloud sessions reporting a foreground fork's Agent call as finished the moment the fork started
  • Fixed local MCP servers seeing a new session ID after a Remote Control session's process restarts
  • Fixed idle compaction being skipped for subscribers still well under their weekly limit
  • Fixed an @-mentioned text file with an extension being silently dropped when even its first 2,000 lines exceed the read limit; Claude is now told its size and how to read it
  • Fixed the plugin "not cached" error pointing to /plugin instead of /reload-plugins, the command that reloads plugins
  • Fixed self-hosted runner sessions failing their first clone under Anthropic-managed git when the machine's git config has an includeIf "gitdir:" or (git 2.44 to 2.46) "onbranch:" section
  • Fixed replies that start with phrases like "You've used" or "You've hit your" showing as a red usage limit error
  • Fixed a resumed conversation sometimes missing its last messages after a crash or kill on Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Foundry and other third-party providers
  • Fixed NotebookEdit saving an invalid notebook when an edit changes a cell's type; turning a cell with attachments into code is now refused
  • Fixed a long README in a design system moved from standalone Claude Design losing its list of files to load when Claude starts a deck or design
  • Fixed MCP tool calls failing with "malformed task handle" when the server's task ID is longer than 128 characters; IDs of up to 1,024 characters now work
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed --configure-git sometimes reporting a hung git --version as a git that isn't on PATH
  • Fixed task ids being reused and deleted tasks coming back when several tasks were deleted or updated at once, and TaskGet listing completed tasks as blockers
  • Fixed stale and repeated rows in the fullscreen Ctrl+R history picker when prompts share a timestamp
  • Fixed Code Mode silently skipping a tool call whose input has a list of over 4,096 items, and freezing on a very large typed array in a tool's input, which is now refused
  • Fixed Code Mode leaving a message unanswered when it was typed during a command and Esc was pressed before Claude replied; the message now starts a new turn, which a second Esc stops
  • Fixed Code Mode not telling Claude when a slow command moved to the background and left its script with empty output, or of the time limit on background commands in claude -p and the Agent SDK
  • Fixed Code Mode sometimes waiting for minutes on a command that had already been stopped
  • Fixed a typed slash command's inline shell commands not running in Code Mode after a background script's output arrived
  • Fixed Code Mode sessions in the Agent SDK and claude -p sometimes losing Claude's last reply on resume after being stopped while a script was running
  • Remote Control: Fixed sessions hosted by the desktop app or VS Code showing as idle while /compact runs
  • Fixed a session sometimes losing its "needs input" status after a background task's report in Claude Desktop
  • Fixed Grep: -o missing an empty match at the end of a file with no last newline, -o with multiline adding an empty line or misnumbering lines in non-UTF-8 files, and -A and -B ignored beside a zero -C
  • Fixed unbinding a chord in keybindings.json still leaving its first key waiting for a second when it was spelled meta and bound as alt, or the reverse
  • Fixed moving an empty session to the background sometimes failing with "Couldn't load transcript from file"
  • Fixed OpenTelemetry reporting a failed mcp_server_connection event at each start for a built-in server that isn't turned on for the account
  • Fixed Esc not stopping a Bash command while it waited for its file diff in large or slow git repositories, which held the next message
  • Fixed pasted links and relative paths ending in an image file name appearing late and swallowing an Enter pressed right after
  • Fixed /mcp reconnect all and /mcp disable all counting a built-in server that isn't turned on for the account
  • Fixed interrupting a turn while a mod's turn.step hook was waiting showing "user-cancel" as an error instead of "Interrupted"
  • Fixed ~/.claude.json being reported as corrupted when another session was in the middle of saving it
  • Fixed web searches failing with an API error when Claude's list of allowed or blocked domains was empty or had duplicates
  • Fixed resuming a paused workflow in Code Mode waiting for minutes while other background work was running
  • Fixed subagents in Code Mode failing with "Agent stalled" and losing their command when a script ran for more than 10 minutes
  • Improved claude plugin marketplace add on Windows to wait and try again in some cases when another program, such as a virus scanner, briefly holds the downloaded files
  • Windows: Improved stability on some company PCs, where Claude Code could exit with no output shortly after start
  • Improved computer use setup: the Screen Recording permission prompt can now restart Claude Code and resume the chat
  • Improved computer use to take less context until Claude uses it
  • Improved the error when a proxy or gateway cuts or damages a compressed response: a turn now ends in plain words instead of raw "ZlibError fetching" text
  • Improved /context: shorter output in fullscreen, so the total is less likely to scroll off in a short window, and the legend names its unit once
  • Improved peak memory use and speed of /usage on machines with many recent sessions
  • Improved /permissions to refuse a rule that would be skipped at the next start, such as rm -rf with no tool name, and to show the reason
  • Improved resuming a session in Code Mode: Claude is now told up front that its earlier script variables are gone
  • Improved Claude in Code Mode to confirm before discarding worktree changes, to read artifact files before publishing them, and to update an existing artifact instead of creating a second one
  • Improved Code Mode's tool search to show long MCP tool descriptions whole where they fit, as a cut description could lead to wrong calls
  • Linux: Improved the Ctrl+V message to name the package to install (wl-clipboard or xclip) when images can't be read from the clipboard
  • Improved recovery for long conversations behind a proxy or gateway with a request size limit, where every message and /compact failed with a 413
  • Improved Glob speed in large local folders on Windows machines with 6 or more CPUs: folders are walked in parallel, and a search stopped at its time limit now lists what it found
  • Improved memory use when resuming a long conversation
  • Improved memory use at startup with MCP servers that list many tools
  • Improved memory use of claude -p and SDK-hosted sessions at the start of a conversation
  • Updated computer use on macOS to newer safety rules, so some actions are refused and typing can be slower
  • Changed terminal and VS Code sessions moved to Sonnet 5 or 5.5 on Bedrock Mantle, Agent Platform and Foundry to start in auto mode if no mode is set; set disableAutoMode to "disable" to stop it
  • Changed the sonnet model alias on Google Cloud's Agent Platform and Microsoft Foundry to Sonnet 5.5, and Foundry's opus alias to Opus 5.5; sonnet on Amazon Bedrock stays at Sonnet 4.5
  • Changed the default model on Microsoft Foundry to Sonnet 5.5: deploy claude-sonnet-5-5, or set ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL to a model you have deployed
  • Changed sonnet and background requests on Google Cloud's Agent Platform to read VERTEX_REGION_CLAUDE_5_5_SONNET; with only the 4_5 variable set they go to CLOUD_ML_REGION or us-east5
  • Changed --model default and a Default pick to move to an older model when that model isn't available, instead of stopping with an error; in auto mode, only to a model auto mode accepts
  • Changed Microsoft Foundry: Claude Sonnet 4, Opus 4 and Opus 4.1 now count as retired, so step-downs stop above them and a pin to one warns that it was retired
  • Changed the Claude apps gateway's built-in model list: Sonnet 5.5 replaces Sonnet 4.5 as its second model, and Claude Desktop starts on it where a policy allows no Opus 4.6
  • Changed SDK and claude -p mid-turn messages to count as the user's where feature flags aren't fetched, as on clouds or with telemetry off, from Opus 4.8 on; mark relayed text isSynthetic: true
  • Changed computer-use to a reserved skill name on Macs with computer use on: your own skill or command of that name stops loading, and a start-up notice says to rename it
  • Changed the default OpenTelemetry service.name of desktop Code tab sessions to claude-code-desktop; update filters keyed on claude-code, or set OTEL_SERVICE_NAME to keep the old name
  • Changed OpenTelemetry tool_input to show only the length of text sent through SendUserMessage or Cowork's message tool, unless response logging is on (OTEL_LOG_ASSISTANT_RESPONSES=1)
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN: its prefix can now end in oat02- as well as oat01-. Update proxy rules and log scrubbers that match oat01-, and mask the whole value
  • Changed claude self-hosted-runner setup with no arguments on macOS and Linux to ask for the environment key in the terminal before Claude starts, and to hide it as you paste
  • Changed Claude Desktop's Code tab on Anthropic's API to ignore default, side-request, alias and subagent model ids not starting with claude in your own settings beside a gateway address
  • Changed Claude Desktop's Code tab on Anthropic's API to ignore a CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW under 200K in your own settings beside a gateway address; use /autocompact instead
  • Changed plan mode in the desktop app's Code tab and VS Code to ask for approval instead of refusing when no auto mode safety check can judge a command, for plans entered from Manual or Accept edits
  • Changed PgUp and Home to go to No on destructive questions, such as /clear from an agent's view
  • Changed /feedback drafts in the terminal to open on Not now, above separate rows to send the report alone or with the transcript
  • Changed tap-mode voice dictation to keep the microphone on until 60 seconds without new words or 10 minutes, up from 15 seconds and 2 minutes, then keep the text unsent; the next tap adds to it
  • Changed tap-mode voice dictation to stop when you send the prompt, and to stop and say why when you edit it, a panel covers it, or the connection or a separate recorder program is lost
  • Changed /schedule, permission prompts and /loop's cloud offer to say "cloud scheduled task" instead of "routine" or "cloud schedule"; /routines still works
  • Changed model switches from the Claude mobile app or claude.ai to keep the effort level you saved for the previous model when none is saved for the new one
  • Changed the hint a mod's PromptHint hook receives to leave out the hint for selected text when the fullscreen footer has a label on its right
  • Changed awsCredentialExport to time out after 10 minutes instead of waiting forever
  • [VSCode] Added a notification in more cases when closing a proposed diff leaves the edit unapplied, and stopped the diff notifications on a split copy of an answered diff
  • [VSCode] Added a warning when restoring a conversation with /rewind in the side bar stops a self-paced /loop
  • [VSCode] Added the installed version to the rows of Manage plugins
  • [VSCode] Fixed Rewind staying on "Checking code changes…" while Claude's process hung at its start
  • [VSCode] Fixed the model picker's arrow keys starting from the wrong row right after it opens, and screen readers not announcing its highlighted model when opened with /model or the command menu
  • [VSCode] Fixed the diff view's "Copy deleted line" and "Copy changed line" copying a different line than they name, and a double-click near the bottom copying unasked
  • [VSCode] Fixed the blocked microphone's tooltip being cut off, long addresses running out of Web Fetch rows, usage bars looking full in High Contrast, and a Thinking row jumping away when clicked
  • [VSCode] Fixed a second Logout in the same window reporting success while the first was still running, and added a Show logs button to the error when logout fails
  • [VSCode] Fixed the chat showing no notice when a background command, agent, workflow or monitor finished while Claude was idle
  • [VSCode] Fixed forking a conversation, opening and saving memories, and creating project output styles failing on NTFS drives in VS Code 1.101 and 1.102 on Windows 11 24H2 and later
  • [VSCode] Fixed Web Fetch showing "Fetched from" with a success dot when the site returned an error or a redirect that wasn't followed
  • [VSCode] Fixed the compaction summary showing as your own prompt, and in Rewind and prompt history, after reloading, resuming or forking a compacted conversation
  • [VSCode] Fixed spinnerVerbs from Claude Code user and managed settings being ignored
  • [VSCode] Fixed right-to-left text from mods showing its punctuation on the wrong side, and a mod's band or pane filling only part of its width when the panel font has no box-drawing characters
  • [VSCode] Fixed an empty, locked editor pane staying beside the next file or Claude tab after the last Claude tab was closed
  • [VSCode] Fixed a session rename that cannot be saved reverting silently, and screen readers not hearing a session's status, which session is open or which groups are collapsed
  • [VSCode] Fixed a hidden panel's notice not naming the waiting session, Hebrew and Arabic questions reading out of order, and a question cut off when Claude's process ended showing only a red dot
  • [VSCode] Fixed a sign-in that failed with no error message returning to the sign-in screen with nothing shown, and an authentication error still looking current after you signed in again in that tab
  • [VSCode] Fixed the chat moving when a menu opened over some banners, and an agent's tool call count shrinking in long sessions; it now shows how many of the calls are listed
  • [VSCode] Fixed most links to files without an extension, to folders, and with a line and column doing nothing
  • [VSCode] Fixed queued messages and attached files showing in reverse order after a conversation was reopened
  • [VSCode] Fixed a question that ended in an error showing "Something went wrong" when its stored result had no text
  • [VSCode] Fixed redacted thinking showing as "Unsupported content type"
  • [VSCode] Fixed the message box not underlining the word that an input method (IME) is composing
  • [VSCode] Fixed a held Up key replacing an unsent message with an earlier prompt, and Down not bringing the message back after the recalled prompt got a new line or was cleared
  • [VSCode] Fixed /model completed with Tab sometimes switching the model, and closing the model picker right away when nothing is running
  • [VSCode] Improved the time it takes to open the Claude panel and long sessions, performance while long replies stream, and the speed of reading diagnostics in very large workspaces
  • [VSCode] Improved commands and one-line output opened in a plain text tab: they now wrap
  • [VSCode] Changed voice dictation to stop by itself after 60 seconds without recognized speech or 10 minutes, up from 15 seconds and 2 minutes, so the microphone can stay on longer
  • [VSCode] Changed voice dictation to stop, and say why, when the microphone stops sending audio or the panel stays hidden

items.title: Data + AI Anywhere: AlloyDB Omni integration with local models
items.summary:
Open models like Gemma 4 from Google DeepMind are a great option to keep your data local. But how can a local AI model integrate with on-premises data?

AlloyDB Omni, Google’s 100% PostgreSQL-compatible database that runs anywhere, now integrates with locally hosted large language models (LLMs). With AlloyDB Omni, you can build agentic experiences on your own infrastructure and on your own terms. Whether it’s in the cloud, in your datacenter, or even on your laptop, you can have data plus AI anywhere.

Built-in AI for your local environment

AlloyDB Omni is a downloadable, run-anywhere edition of AlloyDB that easily deploys to your own infrastructure, including on-premises. AlloyDB Omni packs powerful, built-in AI, including the same ScaNN indexing technology powering Google Search. When you pair AlloyDB Omni with a model, you can store vector embeddings at scale; search them semantically; and even query the database using natural language. You can use virtually any model you like, whether that’s a frontier Cloud-hosted model like Gemini or a local model. And with locally hosted models you maintain complete control over your data environment.

Connecting to Gemma 4, Qwen3.8, and other local models

You can now connect AlloyDB Omni to local models like Gemma 4 and Qwen3.8. No matter which model you choose, the architecture remains the same.

This setup enables entirely new use cases for environments that were previously blocked from adopting agentic capabilities. If you operate an air-gapped network or have data locality requirements, you can still build intelligent applications. You can analyze local logs, generate summaries of proprietary internal documents, and power localized chatbots—all while maintaining strict data governance.

  • Keep data on-premises: Because the database and the model sit in the same local environment, your data never crosses the public internet.

  • Reduce latency: Processing inference requests locally minimizes network transit time.

  • Query directly via SQL: Your standard database queries can invoke machine learning functions that process data locally. Like this:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "SELECT customer_name, ai.generate('Summarize in 1 short sentence: ' || comment, model_id => 'gemma4_llm') AS summary FROM customer_feedback; customer_name | summary ---------------+----------------------------------------------------------------------- Alice | The customer demands a refund for a double charge or they will cancel Bob | The user likes the product but requests dark mode support."), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fe109f54550>)])]>

Next, you’ll see how to run queries like this yourself, step by step.

Get started

You can test this integration on your own machines today. Using a Kubernetes environment we will show you how to deploy and integrate AlloyDB Omni and a local open model.

Step 0: Before you begin

In this example, we will use Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) to host the AlloyDB Omni database and local model. GKE gives us a standardized, reproducible environment but you can use the same setup on-prem or almost anywhere.

We will assume you have already setup:

  1. A GKE cluster, and

  2. Kubernetes tools kubectl and Helm

Step 1: Deploy the AlloyDB Omni Kubernetes Operator

We will use the AlloyDB Omni Kubernetes operator to set up our AlloyDB Omni database. The Operator makes deploying and maintaining AlloyDB Omni a breeze.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "helm install \ cert-manager oci://quay.io/jetstack/charts/cert-manager \ --version v1.21.3 \ --namespace cert-manager \ --create-namespace \ --set crds.enabled=true \ --set global.leaderElection.namespace=cert-manager helm install alloydbomni-operator oci://gcr.io/alloydb-omni/alloydbomni-operator \ --version 1.9.0 \ --create-namespace \ --namespace alloydb-omni-system \ $(helm install --help | grep -q -- '--rollback-on-failure' && echo '--rollback-on-failure' || echo '--atomic') \ --timeout 5m"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fe109f56990>)])]>

Step 2: Create your AlloyDB Omni database

Don’t forget to enable the googleMLExtension.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'kubectl create namespace ai-demo cat << \'EOF\' | kubectl apply -f - apiVersion: v1 kind: Secret metadata: name: db-pw-my-omni namespace: ai-demo type: Opaque data: my-omni: "VmVyeVN0cm9uZ1Bhc3N3b3Jk" # password "VeryStrongPassword" --- apiVersion: alloydbomni.dbadmin.goog/v1 kind: DBCluster metadata: name: my-omni namespace: ai-demo spec: databaseVersion: "18.4.0" primarySpec: adminUser: passwordRef: name: db-pw-my-omni features: googleMLExtension: enabled: true resources: cpu: 2 memory: 4Gi disks: - name: DataDisk size: 20Gi storageClass: standard dbLoadBalancerOptions: annotations: networking.gke.io/load-balancer-type: "internal" allowExternalIncomingTraffic: true EOF'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fe109f56790>)])]>

Step 3: Deploy your AI model

We will use Ollama to help us deploy our model.

In this example we deploy Gemma 4 from Google DeepMind. Or, you can modify this command to deploy Qwen3.8 – just change a few lines as noted in the comments.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'cat << \'EOF\' | kubectl apply -f - apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: ollama namespace: ai-demo spec: replicas: 1 selector: matchLabels: app: ollama template: metadata: labels: app: ollama spec: containers: - name: ollama image: ollama/ollama:latest ports: - containerPort: 11434 env: - name: OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE value: "-1" # keep the model in RAM - name: OLLAMA_LOAD_TIMEOUT value: "20m" resources: requests: cpu: "4" memory: "16Gi" # for Qwen 3.8: 24Gi volumeMounts: - name: models mountPath: /root/.ollama lifecycle: postStart: exec: command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "(sleep 5 && ollama pull gemma4:12b) >/dev/null 2>&1 &"] # For Qwen 3.8, comment out the line above and use this one: # command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "(sleep 5 && ollama pull qwen3.8) >/dev/null 2>&1 &"] volumes: - name: models ephemeral: volumeClaimTemplate: spec: accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"] resources: requests: storage: 30Gi --- apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: ollama-service namespace: ai-demo spec: type: ClusterIP ports: - port: 11434 targetPort: 11434 selector: app: ollama EOF'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fe109f56a10>)])]>

Step 4: Register the model with AlloyDB Omni

Connect to your database.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'kubectl exec -it -n ai-demo $(kubectl get pod -n ai-demo -l alloydbomni.internal.dbadmin.goog/task-type=database -o jsonpath=\'{.items[0].metadata.name}\') -c database -- env PGPASSWORD="VeryStrongPassword" psql -h 127.0.0.1 -U postgres'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fe109f55b10>)])]>

Note: If you receive a connection error, you might need to wait a moment for your database to provision.

Now you should be connected to your AlloyDB Omni database with the psql client. Next, run the following SQL script to register your local model.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS google_ml_integration; ALTER SYSTEM SET google_ml_integration.request_timeout_in_seconds = 600; SELECT pg_reload_conf(); CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION google_ml.ollama_llm_input_transform( model_id character varying, prompt text, generation_config json, system_instructions json ) RETURNS json AS $$ SELECT json_build_object( 'model', CASE model_id WHEN 'gemma4_llm' THEN 'gemma4:12b' WHEN 'qwen3_8_llm' THEN 'qwen3.8' END, 'messages', json_build_array( json_build_object('role', 'system', 'content', COALESCE(system_instructions->'systemInstruction'->'parts'->0->>'text', 'You are a helpful assistant.')), json_build_object('role', 'user', 'content', prompt) ) ); $$ LANGUAGE sql; CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION google_ml.ollama_llm_output_transform( model_id character varying, response json ) RETURNS text AS $$ SELECT trim(regexp_replace( response->'choices'->0->'message'->>'content', '<think>.*?</think>', '', 's')); $$ LANGUAGE sql; CALL google_ml.create_model( model_id => 'gemma4_llm', -- and/or 'qwen3_8_llm', model_request_url => 'http://ollama-service.ai-demo.svc.cluster.local:11434/v1/chat/completions', model_provider => 'custom', model_type => 'llm', model_in_transform_fn => 'google_ml.ollama_llm_input_transform', model_out_transform_fn => 'google_ml.ollama_llm_output_transform' );"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fe109f559d0>)])]>

Note: If you receive a Resource not found error, wait a moment for the model to load.

In addition to registering your model, the above script tells AlloyDB Omni how to interpret the model’s raw output. In this example chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning is part of the response inside <think></think> tags. We don’t want the CoT, so our output transform function removes it.

Step 5: Try it out!

You can use functions like ai.generate built-in to AlloyDB Omni to connect to your local model – without ever leaving the SQL client!

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "CREATE TABLE customer_feedback ( id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, customer_name TEXT, comment TEXT ); INSERT INTO customer_feedback (customer_name, comment) VALUES ('Alice', 'I was charged twice on my credit card! Please refund $49 immediately or I will cancel.'), ('Bob', 'Great product, but can you please add dark mode support?'); SELECT customer_name, ai.generate('Summarize in 1 short sentence: ' || comment, model_id => 'gemma4_llm' /* or 'qwen3_8_llm' */) AS summary FROM customer_feedback;"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fe109f54a10>)])]>

Make it your own

Try out all the AI features that AlloyDB Omni has to offer! AlloyDB Omni supports fast vector search, built-in AI functions, and more. Give them a try and build something great.

items.title: Release 2.75.0 corresponding to NGC container 26.11
items.summary:
Triton Inference Server

The Triton Inference Server provides a cloud inferencing solution optimized for both CPUs and GPUs. The server provides an inference service via an HTTP or GRPC endpoint, allowing remote clients to request inferencing for any model being managed by the server. For edge deployments, Triton Server is also available as a shared library with an API that allows the full functionality of the server to be included directly in an application.

New Features and Improvements

  • PyTorch backend: Added AOTI BF16 input/output support.
  • THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt is now included in the containers.
  • Fixed a use-after-free in the dynamic batcher and a preserve_ordering completion-slot issue on response-cache hits.
  • Prevented silent gRPC stream cancellations under backpressure.
  • Bounded the decompressed HTTP inference response size in the client library.
  • Perf Analyzer: Honored supplied output shapes, propagated the binary exit code, tagged the wheel as platform-specific, and limited profile-data export to the needed inputs and outputs.
  • Python backend: Now logs when the backend stub exits on a crash signal.

Known Issues

  • The Triton TensorRT-LLM Backend container image is not included in this release.
  • vLLM's v0 API and Ray are affected by vulnerabilities. Users should consider their own architecture and mitigation steps which may include but should not be limited to:
    • Do not expose Ray executors and vLLM hosts to a network where any untrusted connections might reach the host.
    • Ensure that only the other vLLM hosts are able to connect to the TCP port used for the XPUB socket. Note that the port used is random.
  • When using Valgrind or other leak detection tools on AGX-Thor or DGX-Spark systems, you might see memory leaks attributed to NvRmGpuLibOpen.
  • Valgrind or other memory leak detection tools may occasionally report leaks related to DCGM. These reports are intermittent and often disappear on retry.
  • CuPy has issues with the CUDA 13 Device API in multithreaded contexts. Avoid using tritonclient cuda_shared_memory APIs in multithreaded environments until fixed by CuPy.
  • TensorRT calibration cache may require size adjustment in some cases, which was observed for the IGX platform.
  • The core Python binding may incur an additional D2H and H2D copy if the backend and frontend both specify device memory to be used for response tensors.
  • A segmentation fault related to DCGM and NSCQ may be encountered during server shutdown on NVSwitch systems. A possible workaround for this issue is to disable the collection of GPU metrics tritonserver --allow-gpu-metrics false ....
  • When using TensorRT models, if auto-complete configuration is disabled and is_non_linear_format_io:true for reformat-free tensors is not provided in the model configuration, the model may not load successfully.
  • When using Python models in decoupled mode, users need to ensure that the ResponseSender goes out of scope or is properly cleaned up before unloading the model to guarantee that the unloading process executes correctly.
  • Triton Inference Server with vLLM backend currently does not support running vLLM models with tensor parallelism sizes greater than 1 and the default "distributed_executor_backend" setting when using explicit model control mode. In attempt to load a vllm model (tp > 1) in explicit mode, users could potentially see failure at initialize step: could not acquire lock for <_io.BufferedWriter name='<stdout>'> at interpreter shutdown, possibly due to daemon threads. For the default model control mode, after server shutdown, vllm related sub-processes are not killed. Related vllm issue: vllm-project/vllm#6766. Please specify "distributed_executor_backend":"ray" in the model.json when deploying vllm models with tensor parallelism > 1.
  • When loading models with file override, multiple model configuration files are not supported. Users must provide the model configuration by setting parameter "config" : "<JSON>" instead of custom configuration file in the following format: "file:configs/<model-config-name>.pbtxt" : "<base64-encoded-file-content>".
  • TensorRT-LLM backend provides limited support of Triton extensions and features.
  • The TensorRT-LLM backend may core dump on server shutdown. This impacts server teardown only and will not impact inferencing.
  • The Java CAPI is known to have intermittent segfaults.
  • Some systems which implement malloc() may not release memory back to the operating system right away causing a false memory leak. This can be mitigated by using a different malloc implementation. Tcmalloc and jemalloc are installed in the Triton container and can be used by specifying the library in LD_PRELOAD. NVIDIA recommends experimenting with both tcmalloc and jemalloc to determine which one works better for your use case.
  • Auto-complete may cause an increase in server start time. To avoid a start time increase, users can provide the full model configuration and launch the server with --disable-auto-complete-config.
  • Auto-complete does not support PyTorch models due to lack of metadata in the model. It can only verify that the number of inputs and the input names matches what is specified in the model configuration. There is no model metadata about the number of outputs and datatypes. Related PyTorch bug: pytorch/pytorch#38273
  • Triton Client PIP wheels for ARM SBSA are not available from PyPI and pip will install an incorrect Jetson version of Triton Client library for Arm SBSA. The correct client wheel file can be pulled directly from the Arm SBSA SDK image and manually installed.
  • Traced models in PyTorch seem to create overflows when int8 tensor values are transformed to int32 on the GPU. Refer to pytorch/pytorch#66930 for more information.
  • Triton cannot retrieve GPU metrics with MIG-enabled GPU devices.
  • Triton metrics might not work if the host machine is running a separate DCGM agent on bare-metal or in a container.

Client Libraries and Examples

The client libraries and examples are available in this release exclusively via the Ubuntu 24.04–based NGC Container. The SDK container includes the client libraries and examples, Performance Analyzer, and Model Analyzer. See Getting the Client Libraries for more information.

ManyLinux Assets (early access)

This release was compiled with AlmaLinux 8.9 based out of manylinux_2_34 and can be used on RHEL 9 and later versions.
See the included README.md for complete details about installation, verification, and support.
This release supports ensembles. Confirm CUDA, TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch, and Python versions in the shipped README.md.
Some optional backend features such as the PyTorch backend's TorchTRT extension are not currently supported.
